title: Shooting victim's kin sue; Carpenter family names police board, ex- chief, officers in $1-million lawsuit
article: A $1-million lawsuit has been filed against Amherstburg's police service alleging one of its officers "acted carelessly, recklessly and with wanton disregard" when he shot and killed Robert Scott Carpenter.
The suit, filed by Carpenter's family, seeks funeral costs, legal costs, loss of potential income costs and punitive damages in the amount of $1,081,843.29.
Plaintiffs in the suit, being handled by Windsor lawyer Patrick Ducharme, include Carpenter's parents, Scott and Janet and Carpenter's two children, Sarah, 5 and Noah, who will turn four Jan. 17.
The suit seeks $375,000 for each child who "witnessed the violent unnecessary death of their father" and will live with the effects of that, potentially for the rest of their lives.

Carpenter's sisters, Sherry Hill, Stacey Belanger and Shelley Dennis, are also listed as plaintiffs. The suit claims the sisters have missed a combined seven months of work because of "emotional stress."

Named as defendants are the town's police services board and since-retired police chief Brian Bird. Also named are the five officers involved in the fatal shooting -- constables Shawn McCurdy, Matt Capel-Cure, Rory Bennett and Viktor Burany and Sgt. Bart DiPasquale.
London's Harrison and Penza law firm is representing the town. It has filed notice it intends to defend the action but has yet to file a statement of defence.

Carpenter, 36, died after he was shot near the groin by McCurdy on Oct. 30, 2000, when police converged on his McCurdy Drive home after receiving a disrupted 911 call from Lisa Stewart, Carpenter's common-law wife.
The province's special investigations unit cleared the officers of any wrongdoing.

A coroner's inquest featuring wildly divergent testimony was told McCurdy fired the fatal shot because Carpenter was attacking DiPasquale with a knife after police entered his home. DiPasquale was not in uniform, but the officers testified they feared for Noah and Sarah because Stewart told them Carpenter was armed with a knife.
The 17 recommendations made by the coroner's jury focused on the failings of Bell Canada's 911 system and did not address issues of police procedure or use of force.

According to the statement of claim, which are allegations not yet proven in court, McCurdy "failed" to use less violent methods such as pepper spray or bodily force to subdue Carpenter and failed to warn Carpenter he might be shot.
The claim alleges that the four other officers "aided and abetted and otherwise facilitated" the assault and battery on Carpenter which was the direct cause of his death.
The plaintiffs further allege that Bird failed to have a qualified crisis negotiator on hand and failed "to ensure the adequate provision of policing to the residents of Amherstburg."
They also allege Bird "failed to monitor, assess and ensure on a regular basis the physical and mental ability of the officers to perform properly their duties."
The same allegations are levelled at the police services board for not having such policies in place.
